title: Making rivals depend on your system is the secret to America's 300-year winning streak
dek: The Dutch, the British, and the Americans took turns as top dog—not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake everything on their maritime system. Once they can't live without your shipping lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
why: Walter Mead breaks down America's 300-year winning formula into a five-step strategy, then pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait, and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.
who: Founders going global and those working in China–US supply chains; engineers studying the Taiwan Strait or drone warfare transformation; investors tracking AI policy risk.

points.h: Unpredictability is a form of power
points.body: ‘Unpredictability’ isn't madness—it's a modern power strategy. Mead says post–Cold War US diplomacy leaned on‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’as a pillar of stability, but Trump profited by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age—the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. Clinton, besieged by the Lewinsky scandal, discovered that shame lives only in other people's minds; as long as you keep moving forward, the dogs bark but the caravan passes. Trump scaled that insight to industrial proportions. The cost is borne by the US diplomatic system: when the world's top power itself becomes the unpredictable card, the alliances and rules built on predictability since WWII accelerate their unraveling.

points.h: The final step of global hegemony is cutting off
points.body: The Anglo-American maritime order won not through any single battle but through a five-step playbook: first, open societies on islands—17th-century Holland tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital flowed in; then global trade—Dutch merchant ships circled the world, and wealth piled up so high that paintings showed Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Step three: while continental powers fought over Silesia inland, you grabbed India and Canada globally. Step four is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain's colonial blockades, invite everyone in to do business—the British navy fought pirates, and all merchant ships benefited; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after their wars. The final step is the trump card: once the other side can't live without your grain, rubber, and shipping lanes, cut them off—Germany in WWI suddenly found Argentine grain and Malayan rubber cut off, and its economy collapsed.

points.h: All of China's efforts are about preventing the umbilical cord from being cut
points.body: Run the same framework over China, and you see Beijing knows exactly where its lifeline lies. Mead says, suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from 100 miles off Taiwan's coast: oil can't get in, manufactured goods can't get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina go void—China's economy would be strangled. He has discussed these scenarios with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always there. So China's energy policy must be read side by side: on one hand, building oil reserves so large they surprise the outside world; on the other, ramping up solar and hydro while mining as much coal as possible. It's not schizophrenia—it's the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the vulnerabilities of‘dependence on the outside world.’He also warns America not to retreat into isolationism—agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to sustain themselves.

points.h: Each wave of technological dividends needs new institutions
points.body: Mead starts with the ownership society: at America's founding, the land was full of independent farmers who owned their plots. Building a bridge might be nice, but it would raise my taxes—that trade-off itself was political education. The railroad era paired with the Homestead Act, as the government gave land to railroad companies and farmers, growing a national market. In the 20th century, the suburban single-family home replaced the family farm, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Today that machine hits the housing wall: young people can't afford to live near work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. If the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable housing land grows with the square of the radius—the physical space technology opens up can support another two generations. But the prerequisite is institutional‘infrastructure’—he coined the term info-structure, meaning the institutional and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courthouses.

points.h: Silicon Valley tilts toward the Tech Hamiltonian camp
points.body: American foreign-policy debate has for centuries been four rhetorics: Hamiltonian—strong government to clear the way for capital; Wilsonian—spread liberal democracy; Jeffersonian—fear of big government; Jacksonian—isolationist in peacetime, but when attacked, fight to the death. The post–Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the tent. Mead says the truly notable new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s, tech companies loved to say‘we're a global company, Google has no borders, Washington can't touch us’; AI competition turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions shifted too: old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets; Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, even wants employees to be patriotic—selling code to China is shameful, and colleagues will report you. The commercial core shifting from old multinationals to tech nationalists is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

points.h: The more equipment a great power has, the more it fears technology transitions
points.body: Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time, at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones that carry mines to blow up tanks; months later, progress was unimaginable. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually with only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is‘how to evacuate the wounded’—you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people out, plus a swarm of drones hunting the enemy's attack drones. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be pulled off the line. The change flips every six months. The irony for America: the power with the most tanks and carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution—existing equipment goes from advantage to relocation cost. The Russian Black Sea Fleet has no major battles to fight, yet it's trapped at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

points.h: The most important new variable in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
points.body: On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment: Beijing needs a very high probability of success to cross the threshold—if it fails, it's catastrophic for the initiator. But between‘attack’and‘do nothing’lies a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade—actions that change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The truly new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is over; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, and reshaping national psychology. Historically, Japan has turned quickly when facing a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor in Japan—that is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

points.h: AI actually makes deterrence more credible
points.body: Applying Cold War deterrence logic to the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive conclusion: deterrence succeeds when the opponent is 100% convinced that‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can and will do it.’As long as the decision chain retains a human veto point—‘I might soften when the moment comes’—the commitment has a crack. Automating part of diplomatic decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into a mechanism that is executable and won't hesitate—deterrence becomes more credible. But that's the doomsday-machine dilemma of science fiction: decisions of civilization-ending scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is‘very interesting and a bit confusing,’and he doesn't think an answer has arrived.

terms.def: A new force in US foreign policy that advocates state power to clear the way for tech companies, replacing old free-market multinational capital.
The institutional, legal, and regulatory framework needed to safely deploy AI in settings like hospitals and courts, as distinct from physical infrastructure.
The American hawkish tradition of staying out of foreign affairs in peacetime but, once attacked, committing to the total destruction of the enemy.
A method of strangling an adversary's trade without direct warfare, using customs, insurance, and port rules to slowly choke it.
